05_marg1832: AND CALLED etc. According to the Seventy: Called again. As according to them God called Beseleel again by name when he commanded the tabernacle to be made according to the pattern which was shown in the mount: so now too he commanded a certain image of the intelligible sacrifices to be described; for this calling again hints at a certain dispensation of things or words looking to higher things.

05_marg1833: AND CALLED etc. HESYCHIUS. By the conjunction he joins what follows to what went before, namely the beginning of this book to the end of the preceding one. For the work of one and the same day is contained in each. The book of Numbers also, because it has nothing between itself and Leviticus, has a like opening, that is: "And the Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai" etc. The people therefore did nothing after the history of Leviticus before the history of Numbers: for they had not changed place, because they had not yet dedicated the tabernacle, nor had much time passed. For in the first month of the second year, at the beginning of the same month, they began to act. But in Exodus and Genesis, because much time had flowed between the death of Joseph and the going out of the children of Israel, the conjunction does not hold the beginning, but a fitting opening is arranged for their dispensation: "These are the names of the children of Israel that went into Egypt."
05_marg1834: AND CALLED etc. In the beginning, setting forth the laws of sacrifices and gifts, he says: If a man offers a gift to God, he shall offer of oxen or of cattle, that is, lambs and kids. But if of birds, turtles or young of the dove. But if not a man but a soul offers a gift to God, let it offer of fine flour unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or fine flour from the frying pan tempered with oil, or from the gridiron. Then he says that leaven ought not to be offered, nor honey mixed with the sacrifices, but every sacrifice or gift salted with salt. Secondly he commands the sacrifices of firstfruits to be offered fresh and cleansed. After these, under the same tenor of the law, he adds concerning the saving sacrifices: first of oxen, secondly of sheep, in which it is lawful to offer, whether lambs or kids, males or females. Nothing besides these did he decree to be offered in the saving sacrifices. But we must see what it is that he said: A man of you etc., as though one not a man could offer, when it would have sufficed to say: If any of you offer. And in what follows he says: If a soul offer a gift. In the later passages, when God speaks a second time to Moses of the sacrifices to be offered for sin, he adds: If the high priest sin, let him offer this or that. But if the whole Synagogue, if a prince, if one soul sin, it is commanded what each is to offer. Let us not think this distinction of persons or things empty. For blessed are the eyes which, the veil of the letter cast away, can see the spirit; and blessed they who bring clean inner ears to hear these things.
05_marg1835: AND CALLED etc. That God does not love the sacrifices of the Jews Isaias shows, saying: To what purpose do you offer me the multitude of your victims, saith the Lord? I am full: I desire not holocausts of rams, and fat of fatlings, and blood of calves and rams and buck goats. Who required these things at your hands? What therefore he had commanded, he refuses. Whence Amos: Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me in the desert? Yet they had often offered them, but those he did not hold pleasing he rejected as though not offered. Hence Jeremias: Eat ye flesh, for I spoke not to your fathers, and I commanded them not concerning the matter of holocausts. But the same who had commanded denies it, because they who had received it passed over the intention of the giver. For the law was subtle, and hidden under the veil of the letter, that those searching it might both amend themselves and understand things to come. The image therefore of rational and intelligible sacrifices is described, and plainly this calling hints at a dispensation of words, or of things looking to higher things.

05_marg1837: THE MAN THAT SHALL OFFER etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The man whom he sets first to offer to the Lord he understands as mankind, which offers the fatted calf, namely that which the father slew for the son who returned after wasting all his substance, made a great feast and had gladness, that the angels in heaven might rejoice over one sinner doing penance. This one, because he had no substance of his own to offer, since he had squandered all, offered the calf sent from heaven; of the herd, that is, of the generation of the Patriarchs; a male, having nothing of womanly frailty; without blemish, "who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth". At the door of the tabernacle, not within, because: "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." He was offered at the door also because he suffered outside the camp, that is, outside the city. For the wicked husbandmen cast the son of the householder out of the vineyard and slew him: here therefore he is offered at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, acceptable before the Lord. For what is so acceptable to God as the victim of Christ, who offered himself? He shall put his hand upon the head, because he laid the sins of mankind upon his own body. For "he is the head of the body, the Church". But perhaps it is not without cause that it was said above, at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and below, at the altar which is at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony; as though it did not suffice to have marked the same place once; but perhaps he wished it to be understood that the blood of Christ was not only shed in Jerusalem, where were the altar and its base and the tabernacle of the testimony, but also sprinkled the altar on high which is in heaven, where is the Church of the firstborn, according to that: He made peace through the blood of his cross, both as to the things on earth and the things that are in heaven; so that the victim was twofold. Paul says to the Hebrews: "through the veil, that is to say, his flesh". And again he interprets the inner veil which Jesus penetrated. If therefore as high priest he entered through two veils, the sacrifice also is twofold, which saves both earthly and heavenly things.

05_marg1839: OF THE HERD A MALE etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. The first sacrifice is the calf, that is, Christ; of the herd, that is, begotten of the stock of the patriarchs; who with the plough of his cross subdued the earth of our flesh, and enriched it with the seed of the Holy Ghost, with the harvest of the virtues.
05_marg1840: The proud calf is our flesh: this we offer when we keep it chaste. At the door of the tabernacle: where it will receive the hearing of divine things. Let the gift be male, let it not know womanly concupiscence; let it flee frailty, dissoluteness and softness. The hand is put upon the victim that it may be acceptable to the Lord, namely the bridle of continence and the hand of discipline, according to that: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. It is slain before the Lord when the members are mortified. The sons of Aaron the priest offer the blood. The priest is in thee, and his sons are thy mind and thy sense, which alone understand the Lord and are capable of his knowledge. He wishes therefore that thou offer a rational sense and thy chaste flesh. Whence: A living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service. For this is the offering of blood at the altar by the priest or his sons, when one is made chaste in body and spirit. For there are those who offer flesh in holocaust not through the ministry of the priest. For not knowingly, nor according to the law which is in the mouth of the priest, are they chaste in body, unchaste in mind. For either they are stained by the lust of glory, or polluted by greed or avarice, or troubled by other vices. For there is not in them the counsel and prudence which perform the priesthood before God; but they are as the foolish virgins, who were chaste in body, but had not the oil of charity and peace and the other virtues.

05_marg1841: IF IT BE A HOLOCAUST etc. HESYCHIUS. Morally. God requires sacrifice that it may profit us, not himself. Whence: I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service etc. The sacrifice pleasing to God therefore is the mortification of our bodies, by which we both abstain from sins and acquire virtues. This some do most fully, others in part: those who mortify themselves wholly and renounce the world become a holocaust, while through the intelligible fire they offer themselves wholly to God, made no longer earthly but heavenly. If therefore such a one has done the justice of the law which is according to the letter, he is fittingly named an ox, who bears the yoke of earthly works, sustaining the law as a yoke, of which Peter says: "Why tempt you God to put a yoke upon the necks" etc.? Paul also says: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Which he expounds thus: Doth God take care for oxen? or doth he say this for our sakes? because he that plougheth should plough in hope. The gift must be male, lest the worker of the law be in any way made womanish. Without blemish, lest he mingle a stain of iniquity or of pretence. At the door of the tabernacle of the testimony: for our conversation ought to be in heaven. In the conscience also dwell the thoughts, which at length bear testimony for us or against us. To make the Lord favourable. But according to the Seventy he says: this acceptable to the offerer; namely, if it be truly acceptable to us, and our heart, judging rightly and clinging to no passion, has proved the gift worthy to be received, then we can pray in the sight of the Lord, that is, obtain remission. Whence: In his sight we shall persuade our hearts, for if our heart reprehend us, we know that God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things etc. And he shall put his hands upon the head of the victim etc. What we call hostia is in Greek called karpoma, in which the intelligible holocaust is signified. For he bears fruit spiritually who through spiritual conversation is made a holocaust: because of which he who offers puts his hand on the head of the victim, which signifies the beginning of the aforesaid conversation, of which he who offers is himself the cause by his promise. For he offers of his own accord, because it is a gift, and every gift is voluntary. For if he transgresses his promise, he accuses himself when he pays the penalty. And thus it will be acceptable and help to his expiation, when by the laying on of the hand he has shown that he offered of his own accord, not of necessity.

05_marg1843: AND HE SHALL IMMOLATE THE CALF etc. HESYCHIUS. For we ought not only to offer our own conscience and conversation to God, but also, as pleases him, by mortifying the body, tending not to lower things but to higher. For this is what the sons of Aaron do before the Lord, slaying and offering the blood; but he who offers is not designated by name. For anyone can bring an offering, that is, promise; but to fulfil the promises, as it were to slay the ox and pour out the blood, belongs to the sons of Aaron alone, by the dignity of the priesthood. And Aaron is interpreted secret or mountainous. Whoever therefore has built himself a temple of God, lofty in virtues, ought to be called a son of Aaron and a priest. For a priest is made by unction, and we are all priests who keep the dignity of the mystic unction. Whence John: "You have the unction from the Holy One." And Peter: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood" etc. These pour out the blood, that is, they do not spare the soul, hearing that: "He that shall lose his soul for me shall find it." For blood signifies the soul, according to that: "The life of the flesh is in the blood." Round about the altar, that is, the Lord's body: because as the sacrifice is laid upon the altar, so the priests work every virtue of the soul upon the body of Christ, that is, in imitation of him. Whence: "You shall make an altar of earth unto me." For the body of Christ is of our earth. And elsewhere: If thou make an altar of stone unto me, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones: for if thou lift up a tool upon it, it shall be defiled. For the flesh of Christ was neither hewn nor smoothed by human hand. At the door of the tabernacle round about, that we may imitate him in all things. And by the door of the tabernacle we understand the apostolic doctrine, by which we enter into the heavenly tabernacle in which God dwells. Whence Isaias: Look down, O Lord, from heaven. As Christ is called the door, so is the apostolic doctrine which he bestows.

05_marg1844: AND WHEN THEY HAVE FLAYED etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The priest draws off the skin by which the members are covered, who separates the veil of the letter from the Word and lays bare the inner members of spiritual understanding, and does not set them in a low place, but on the altar. For he does not open the mysteries to the unworthy and earthly, but to those who are the altar of God, in whom the divine fire is always kindled and the flesh consumed. He divides the calf limb by limb who explains in order and distinctly what is the progress: to have touched the hem of Christ, to have washed his feet with tears and wiped them with the hair, and how much more to have anointed his head, or what prerogative it has to have leaned upon his breast; to set out the reasons of these. To fit some things to beginners, others to those advancing in the faith of Christ, others to those already perfect in knowledge and charity: this is the dismembering of the calf. He also who knows how to show what are the beginnings of the law, what the progress in the prophets, what the perfection in the Gospels; with what milk little ones are nourished, with what oil the weak are cherished, with what solid food the athletes of Christ are fattened. He fittingly arranges the holocaust of the calf by distinct members, and puts wood under the altar for the fire to burn, who shows not only the bodily virtues of Christ, but in some measure his Godhead. For the Godhead of Christ is from above, whither this fire hastens. Fittingly therefore the heavenly fire consumed all things that were done in the body of the Saviour, and restored all to the nature of his Godhead. Yet this fire is kindled with wood applied: for he suffered even to the cross; but when he was hung on the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was ended. For rising from the dead he ascended into heaven, which way of his the nature of fire shows. Whence: If we have known Christ according to the flesh; but now we know him so no longer. For the holocaust of his flesh, offered through the wood of the cross, joined earthly things to heavenly and human to divine. Morally. He commands the entrails with the feet to be washed with water, in signification of baptism. He washes the entrails who cleanses the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the consummation of the sacrament. For he that is clean needeth not but to wash his feet, but is clean wholly; nor can anyone have part with Jesus unless he has washed his feet.
05_marg1845: Morally. AND WHEN THEY HAVE FLAYED etc. The skin is drawn off when we are stripped of riches and of all worldly things. Whence: Skin for skin, and all that a man hath he will give for his life. The members are cut up when the conversation of each is built up to the increase of the body in the measure of the member. The sons of Aaron put fire under when they kindle the spirit, laying in order a pile of wood, namely the meditations and teachings of the Scriptures, by which the Spirit of God is nourished and continually kindled, that it be quenched by no whirlwinds. Whence: "Extinguish not the spirit. Despise not prophecies." And by the pieces we understand the soul and body. For though they are of one living being, they are set against each other. The flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh etc. And the head signifies the mind. Whence Isaias: "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is sad." For these are said to suffer with each other, and our rational part, dwelling in both, is cherished in the health of both. The head is not divided, because the mind ought not to wander through divers things, but be guarded by the peace of God, according to that: The peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts etc. All things that cleave to the liver, or the fat according to the Seventy, by which namely the appetites of the desires are moved. For it lies over the kidneys and the groin, which are the organs of coition. And these we offer when we use the desires not bodily but spiritually. We lay them on the altar with wood put under, that we may fit them to the spiritual Scriptures which were spoken of the altar of the Lord's body. The entrails, that is, the hidden thoughts, being washed with the water of baptism or the tears of penance, and the feet, that is, the actions. Upon the altar: in this it becomes a sweet savour to the Lord. Our sacrifice becomes a holocaust to the Lord and an odour of sweetness when we offer all things upon the intelligible altar, imitating Christ as far as we can.
05_marg1846: Morally. And when they have flayed etc. We draw the skin off the victim when we remove the surface of virtue from the eyes of the mind. We cut the joints into pieces when, distinguishing finely and limb by limb, we consider its inward parts. If we are sometimes afflicted by the impulse of unlawful thought, it is for this reason, that we are gladly busied in certain acts of earthly thought, though lawful. And when earthly action is touched by desire even in the least things, the strength of the devil growing, our mind is defiled by temptation. Whence the members of the victim, cut into pieces, the head and the things about the liver, are commanded to be burned with fire, but the feet and entrails first to be washed with water. For we offer ourselves a sacrifice to God when we immolate the works of our life, distinguishing them by virtues. We burn the head and the things contained about the liver when in our sense, by which the whole body is ruled, and in our hidden desires, we burn with the flame of divine love. And yet it is commanded that the feet and entrails be washed: for by the feet the earth is touched, by the entrails dung is carried; because often, already kindled by desire for eternity, we gape with the whole sense of devotion after the appetite of our mortification. But because we still do something earthly through infirmity, we also bear in the heart many unlawful things which we have already subdued. And when unclean temptation defiles our thoughts, the entrails of the victim carry dung. But that they may be burned, they are washed, because weeping washes away the unclean thoughts, which heavenly love may burn in the acceptance of the sacrifice. And whatever the mind suffers, whether in the struggle it has experienced or from the memory of its former conversation, is washed, that it may burn the more sweetly in the sight of God the more it has begun to stand before him, laying nothing earthly, nothing slippery, in the ark of its prayer.

05_marg1847: AND IF OF THE FLOCKS etc. HESYCHIUS. With a few things changed, he says the same. And it is to be noted that he commanded the Israelite to offer not only of oxen but also of sheep. 05_marg1850: AND HE SHALL IMMOLATE IT AT THE SIDE etc. HESYCHIUS. This he did not command concerning the oxen, but that they be immolated before the Lord. Whence the words seem to have contrariety and difference, since both are a holocaust but have a different place. According to the letter, therefore, he gave the same place to both. For the altar of holocausts was set before the tabernacle at the side of the door, that the entrance to the holies might not be blocked for those ministering, as is said in Exodus: And he put the veil at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and he set the altar of holocausts about the door of the tabernacle. Whatever therefore was offered for sacrifice stood at the side of the altar on the north, and so the sacrifice was celebrated before the Lord, that is, in sight of the holies: for the holy of holies is called the face of God, because the glory of God dwelt in it. Whence the priest was commanded to enter into it once a year. The difference of the words therefore was necessary for contemplation. For the altar is Christ; the sheep, those who study simplicity. The offering of sheep, therefore, is not offered simply straight before the intelligible altar, as that of oxen, but at the side. For he offers straight on who fulfils the commandments; but at the side he who abstains from evils; as into a royal hall it is better to enter by the straight door, yet it is good to enter even from the side. For to offer to God in any manner is good. To the north he necessarily added. For this part is almost always cloudy. For those are darkened by cloud, that is, ignorance, who give themselves wholly to innocence; therefore it is called a holocaust even without the working of justice.

05_marg1852: BUT IF OF BIRDS etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. The turtle is the flesh of Christ, according to that of Solomon: "Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's." The dove signifies the Holy Ghost. Whence: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending as a dove, this is my Son. The turtle and the dove therefore are the flesh of Christ joined to the Spirit. These three sacrifices the man, that is, Christ, offers: namely of oxen, of cattle and of birds.
05_marg1853: Wonderful is the subtlety of the words, not only because it describes the differences of ways of life, but signifies some according to the law, some above the law. For the offerings of oxen and sheep are according to the law, though they are called voluntary; because even if to offer is in the power of the offerer (for man is of free will), yet not what sort he works. It is necessary therefore either to offer an ox or a sheep, that is, either to work justice or to abstain from evils. Whence above: The man among you that shall offer a sacrifice to the Lord of the cattle, that is, of oxen and sheep, shall offer victims. But birds are not numbered with the aforesaid offering. For this sacrifice is more perfect and greater, and of few. For the birds are men given to contemplation, who, if of necessity they mix themselves in earthly business, soon fly back to heavenly things. Whence: They sow not, neither do they reap, and your heavenly Father feedeth them. Let such a one offer of turtles and doves, that is, in knowledge and spiritual meekness, that the knowledge of the law may not exceed, busied in vain things: for the turtle signifies knowledge. Whence Jeremias: "The turtle, and the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming: but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord." And the dove, clean and simple, signifies the Holy Ghost and declares what they ought to be who study to contemplate the holy Scriptures. Whence Ezechias: I will meditate like a dove. One priest offers, not many, because contemplation is of few. Whence he offers at the altar, while the rest are offered at the tabernacle of the testimony. For contemplatives put earthly things after, contemplate and savour heavenly things, "where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God".

05_marg1860: Allegorically. The soul offers the fourth sacrifice. The fine flour signifies the Church, which is gathered from many persons as from grains, separated by the mill of the law and the Gospel between the letter and the spirit, united through the water of baptism, anointed with chrism, and made solid by spiritual fire; through humility it becomes an acceptable victim.
05_marg1861: ORIGEN. A soul etc. Namely one which has neither calf, nor sheep, nor kid, nor a pair of turtles or two young pigeons: this is the sensual man, who, if he is not pressed by sins nor cast headlong through vices, yet has nothing spiritual in himself, or, figuratively, the flesh of the Word of God. The sensual man perceiveth not the things that are of the Spirit of God; but the spiritual man judgeth all things. This one therefore who is named a soul cannot offer all things, because he cannot examine all things; but only fine flour and unleavened loaves, that is, this common life in husbandry and in the other uses of life. Yet he offers fine flour tempered with oil. For every soul needs the oil of divine mercy or grace.
05_marg1862: HESYCHIUS. A soul when it shall offer etc. The soul signifies the whole man, as there: "All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt" etc. And Luke says: And we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls. Perhaps by the soul he signifies the Gentile. For above he commanded the children of Israel to offer sacrifices with blood. But here, commanding him who is without the law to offer, he does not say 'man', as above, but soul. The Gentile was sensual, not understanding the things that are of God; but the mercy of God calls him to the offering, that he may receive salvation, when he arranges sacrifices for sins; he who has neither sheep nor goat, he commands to offer a turtle or a dove; he who has not that, fine flour. For he is saved no longer by works, as one poor in virtues, but by the knowledge of God alone, which, though it is the beginning of salvation, yet frankincense and oil are to be put upon it, that the grace of God may be mingled with alms and prayers. Whence the angel says to Cornelius: Thy prayers and thy alms are ascended before the Lord. In frankincense the inner passions are cured, and by its smoke eyes that water from infirmity are healed. For prayer heals the passions of the soul, cures the inner eyes of ignorance, and drives away the tears that rise from the sickness of sin.
05_marg1863: The ministers of the Church. Because whatever we offer we ought to confer with the holy doctors of the Church. Whence Paul conferred the Gospel with the apostles, lest he had run in vain.

05_marg1864: AND ONE OF THEM etc. The unity of the Church takes a handful of the flour, because according to the capacity of his sense each of the faithful ought to seek the knowledge of Scripture. Whence: "Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety."
05_marg1865: MORALLY. And one of them etc. It is to be noted that a handful of the flour and oil, but all the frankincense, is commanded to be offered, because wisdom, which is marked in the flour, and charity or mercy, which is marked in the oil, cannot be full in this life. Whence: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner"; and "now I know in part" etc. A part of the oil also is offered, because mercy is never fulfilled; for even if thou have mercy as much as thou canst, yet thou oughtest to wish more. Charity also, which is figured by oil, is begun in the present and will be perfected in the future. But all the frankincense is burned, because one perseveres always in prayer.
05_marg1866: Of knowledge or of the acquaintance of God. For that knowledge is acceptable to God which faith can grasp; and as he who wishes to grasp more in a handful gains nothing, for all runs out, so faith is the measure of the knowledge of God. 05_marg1869: BUT WHEN THOU OFFEREST etc. HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. The sacrifice is Christ immolated for us. Baked in the oven: namely in the virgin's womb. For the oven receives bread and fire: so the virgin's womb received from heaven the bread of life, that is, the Word of God, and the fire of the Holy Ghost. Whence: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" etc. If therefore thou offerest the gift of the incarnation of Christ, which was made in the virgin's womb, it is not acceptable to God unless it be made of fine flour, that is, of the knowledge or acquaintance of God. For of this matter we receive the speech from the apostles and from the prophets. The words of the apostles are loaves, of the prophets wafers. For as loaves are fitter than wafers for nourishing, so much do the words of the apostles excel the words of the prophets. And both are unleavened, without the leaven of worldly knowledge. Yet both are made in oil: for with one accord it was written by them of Christ's mercy; because the apostles and prophets wrote, but the apostles wrote more fully, who showed fulfilled what those announced as to come.
05_marg1870: A broad and thin bread, which signifies prophecy and the law: for as much as the solidity of bread differs from the thinness of the wafer, so much the Gospel from the words of the law and the prophets. To offer sacrifice from the fryingpan therefore is to discourse with veneration of the mystery of the cross.

05_marg1872: IF THY OBLATION etc. HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. The oblation from the fryingpan is the dispensation of the passion from the cross. The fryingpan is consumed by fire, and renders the foods laid upon it fit for eating either at once or after a long interval; the cross also, strong above all things, subjected every creature to the crucified, and made the flesh fit which before the passion did not seem fit for eating. For if he had not been crucified, we should not eat the sacrifice of his body, which we now do in memory of his passion. Whence it is said to Ezechiel: Take unto thee a frying pan of iron, and thou shalt set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city: namely Jerusalem, which was most offended at the cross of the Lord, and therefore withdrew from the knowledge of him. OF FLOUR TEMPERED WITH OIL: because he died and had mercy on us. WITHOUT LEAVEN: without stain. THOU SHALT DIVIDE IT INTO LITTLE PIECES: that we may divide the discourse of his sufferings, which proceeded by parts, and diligently distinguish the blows, namely the buffets, the spittle and the wounds. AND THOU SHALT POUR OIL UPON IT: that as he died mercifully for us, we too may have mercy on our brethren even unto death.

05_marg1873: AND IF etc. HESYCHIUS. As in the fryingpan we take the cross, so in the gridiron the death and burial. For the fryingpan is put over a fire burning and kindled, but the gridiron over coals burning and kindled long before: so the death of Christ was not the beginning of the passion, but its continuance. This gift is made of fine flour, that is, of the knowledge of God. For Christ who died according to the flesh must be preached God and immortal. The gift is made in oil, because he who discourses of both the death and the resurrection must add mercy also: for out of mercy he bore death and dispensed the resurrection.
05_marg1874: And if etc. He offers fine flour who studies to live well in some of the uses of common life. This is to be tempered with oil, because every soul needs the oil of mercy, nor can it escape the present life unless heavenly mercy be present. 05_marg1875: ORIGEN. Someone may say: It went almost better with the ancients, to whom pardon was granted by divers sacrifices; with us there is only one pardon of sins, through the laver of baptism; after sin, no mercy. For it befits the Christian, for whom Christ died, to be of stricter discipline: oxen, goats and sheep were slain, and birds, and fine flour was tempered with oil; for thee the Son of God was slain, and does it delight thee to sin again? Yet do not despair: thou hast heard how many sacrifices for sins there are in the law; hear how many remissions there are in the Gospels. The first is in baptism. The second is in martyrdom. The third through almsgiving. Whence: Give what you have, and behold all things are clean unto you. The fourth, because we forgive our brethren. Whence: If you forgive your brethren from your hearts, your Father also will forgive you etc. The fifth, because we convert "a sinner from the error of his way", according to that: "He who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way" etc. The sixth through abundance of charity. Whence it is said: Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. And elsewhere: "Charity covereth a multitude of sins." The seventh through hard and laborious penance, when the sinner washes his bed with tears, and they become his bread day and night, and he is not ashamed to confess his sin to the priest of the Lord and seek medicine, according to him who says: "I said: I will confess against myself" etc. Hence James: Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the Church. Thou therefore, when thou comest to the grace of baptism, hast offered a calf, because thou art baptized in the death of Christ. When thou art led to martyrdom, thou hast offered a goat, because thou hast slain the devil, the author of sin. When thou hast done alms and spent the affection of mercy on the needy, thou hast honoured the holy altar with fat kids. If thou hast forgiven thy brother from the heart, and laid aside the swelling of anger, and had a meek and simple mind, thou hast sacrificed a ram or a lamb. If, instructed by the divine readings, meditating like a dove, and watching in the law of the Lord, thou hast converted a sinner from the error of his way and called him back to the simplicity of the dove, and, joining him to the saints, made him imitate the fellowship of the turtle, thou hast offered a pair of turtles or two young pigeons. But if thou hast loved thy neighbour not only as thyself, but as Christ, who says: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends etc., know that thou hast offered unleavened loaves of fine flour, worked with the oil of charity, without the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. If thou hast been in the bitterness of weeping, if thou hast wasted thy flesh and dried it up with much abstinence, so as to say: My bones are grown dry like fuel for the fire, thou hast offered in sacrifice fine flour from the fryingpan or from the gridiron. In this way thou offerest more truly and perfectly, according to the Gospel, the sacrifices which Israel can no longer offer according to the law.
05_marg1876: Nothing voluptuous, nothing sweet pleases God, but what has something of sharpness and severity. Whence the Pasch is eaten with bitter herbs.
05_marg1877: Of Gentile eloquence, which is sweet in sound, not in substance. Whence: The lips of a harlot are like a honeycomb dropping. But what is said in the Canticles, "Honey and milk are under thy tongue", does not contradict the present words. For it says 'under the tongue', not 'on the tongue', to show that the wisdom of the pagans and the letter of the Jews are subject to the tongue of the Church, that is, to its doctrine. He does not wish the whole doctrine of these to be offered. Whence he says: It shall not be burnt in the sacrifice, that is, the holocaust: you shall offer only their firstfruits. For we offer the firstfruits of that wisdom, not the whole, as Paul says to the Athenians: As some also of your own poets said, For we are also his offspring. For what he found fitting to the knowledge of God he did not reject; yet he did not multiply testimonies further, because "it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe". Whence Moses says: But they shall not be put upon the altar; and though it might have been said they shall not be placed, he says: They shall not be put upon it for a savour of sweetness; signifying that if we try to gain the knowledge of the Godhead from outward things, such a sacrifice does not ascend to the altar, but is pressed down among earthly things, because it is of the earth.

05_marg1878: THOU SHALT SEASON IT WITH SALT etc. Apostolic wisdom. Whence: "You are the salt of the earth" etc. As every food is seasoned with salt, so is the word of preaching with apostolic doctrine. Therefore salt is commanded to be offered in every sacrifice, that we may live according to the apostolic doctrine and institution and the imitation of its work. Whence Paul says: "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ." And elsewhere: "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets." Whence also the lawgiver did not say simply salt, but the salt of the covenant of thy God. For as the covenant is rational, so also the salt is rational. He wished therefore to remind us of the Gospel testament and the apostolic salt. Oil is offered in the sacrifice if we offer with cheerfulness, not out of sadness or of necessity. "For God loveth a cheerful giver."

05_marg1879: BUT IF THOU OFFER A GIFT OF THE FIRSTFRUITS etc. ORIGEN. In the second place the offering of the firstfruits, that is, of the beginnings, of the corn is commanded, which the law of God bade to be done on the day of Pentecost: but to them the shadow was given, for us the truth was reserved. And on the day of Pentecost, the sacrifice of prayers being offered, the Church received the firstfruits of the Holy Ghost, the apostles. And truly these were fresh, because it was new. Whence also they were said to be "full of new wine". Dried at the fire: for fiery tongues sat upon every one of them.
05_marg1880: HESYCHIUS. But if thou offer etc. He commands not only those who have remained in it to offer the acquaintance or knowledge of God, but the untaught also. Whence the Apostle: Immediately, when he was called, he preached. He is a firstfruit to God who has newly begun to believe, who formerly offered him no fruit of knowledge. Such ones, because they do not yet bring forth the mysteries finely so as to offer meal or fine flour, must offer things green and dried and broken. For as with moist fruits, not yet fit for the mill to become meal or fine flour, we break them with fire and separate the chaff: so those who do not yet have solid knowledge nor subtle theology need the fire of the Holy Ghost, that they may separate the chaff of the letter, whereby they may possess sufficient knowledge of God. And we must pour oil over it and put on frankincense: for through almsgiving and prayer divine knowledge is perfected in us.

05_interl5145: ORIGEN. The saving offering, which is offered only of oxen and sheep or goats. For for sins the soul is commanded generally to offer; but after this it goes through various persons, so that if the high priest offend and offer for sin, he shall offer a calf, not as for a gift.

05_marg1881: WHETHER MALE OR FEMALE etc. HESYCHIUS. Above, only males are offered in holocaust. By the holocaust therefore the highest virtues are designated: namely to be a virgin, to renounce the world, and the like, which are the sacrifices of few. But the victims of peace offerings are the lesser virtues and the common vows of the faithful, by which God is appeased. Whence females are offered with males, that is, weak works with stronger.
05_interl5150: in the good pleasure of the Lord
05_marg1882: AND IF HIS OBLATION BE A SACRIFICE etc. ORIGEN. Passing over the rest, he speaks of the saving sacrifices which are offered of animals, that is, oxen and goats and sheep, and nothing further is substituted for immolation; not even birds, which were substituted above in the offering of gifts. For he who offers saving victims is already conscious of his salvation. He must therefore offer great and perfect things. Whence the Apostle: "But strong meat is for the perfect."
05_marg1883: HESYCHIUS. And if his oblation be a sacrifice etc. According to the laws there are divers ways of life of men; there are virtues ordered in the manner of ladders, so that one attains some, another all, that each may be raised from the earth; which the difference of the sacrifices signifies. Whence here one offers a holocaust, that is, himself wholly, as Paul, who is nailed to the cross with Christ; another the sacrifice of peace offerings, or the saving sacrifice, who desires salvation but cannot ascend to lofty things. For he who cannot be a virgin, if he lives in holy wedlock, receives life from the Lord who says: "All men take not this word", and is necessarily ranked among the saved. So also of the contempt of things, of justice, of taking food with thanksgiving. For he is great who does great things; small, not least, he who can attain salvation, namely by middling things. According to the two kinds of ways of life therefore, he sets two definitions of voluntary sacrifices. For he says in Exodus: You shall make an altar of earth unto me, and you shall offer upon it your holocausts and peace offerings, your sheep and oxen etc. He adds the peace offerings as of the second rank and virtue. He therefore who thinks it suffices him if he be saved, offers indeed of the oxen. And the oxen are those who do the things of the law; he offers a gift, male and female, without blemish. But he does not command him who offers a holocaust to offer a female; not that the female is deprived of the way of life, but because to savour perfect things belongs to men, that is, to the stronger. Whence: "Who shall find a valiant woman?" For strength is scarcely found in women. The sacrifice of peace offerings is of men and of women: for they must live worthily that they may come to salvation.

05_marg1884: HESYCHIUS. The intelligible fat must be offered, that is, desire, which the Greeks call epithymia, which covers first the upper belly, then the lower, that we may offer the desire both of thinking and of doing: for thought goes before, fulfilment follows. And this we do in the belly, that is, in the heart, in which we first set before us actions as though we craved them; then we hasten to accomplish them as though we digested them. Let us therefore propose nothing wicked, fulfil nothing. And well does he describe the fat which covers the belly over the upper belly, that is, the appetite, since the greatest part of desire is about the appetite or purpose. And to the lower belly he joined the two kidneys, because there is a certain kinship of the kidneys and the heart. Whence: "Burn my reins and my heart." Elsewhere also they are joined: Who triest the reins and the hearts. For physicians set the motion of anger in the heart, but say that the memory of this thing lies in the kidneys, in which the female also is the cause; whence also they have communion with the thighs. He wishes therefore the desire of marriage also to be offered to God, that it may be for the sake of offspring, not of fornication, that marriage may be honourable and the bed undefiled. Let us offer anger also to God, that we may be angry against sin. Whence: "Be angry, and sin not." Hence Moses, being very angry, cast down the tables and broke them. And because concupiscence is in the liver, he commands the lobe, that is, the top, to be taken away and offered with the kidneys: that we may offer to God the firstfruits of our thoughts, and sanctify the lump by the first portion.

05_marg1885: The Seventy: The belly, that is, the heart. Of which it makes mention a second time according to the Seventy, because according to the physicians it has a twofold working: by one part it draws in nourishment, which they call the upper belly; by the other it separates the purgation, which they call the lower belly. The kidneys are the ministers of the genital seeds, communicating with the belly and the thighs. He commands therefore to be offered first the fat which is over the belly, and the two kidneys, and the fat which is over them, that is, over the thighs, which are near the kidneys: for they are placed in the middle between the thigh and the belly.

05_marg1887: AND THE RUMP etc. The Seventy: The loin whole without blemish, namely that one thing be not offered to God and another to the adversary. For it suffices this one for pardon not to do the things that are of virtue; but if he works evil, he does not obtain pardon. Whence: Be ye simple as doves. For doves have exceeding simplicity, no malice. He who offers sacrifice of the oxen does not need to offer the loin to God, which he binds up and exercises in good works. He who immolates of the goats has no loin without blemish to offer, because he once stained it with sin. He therefore who was not in sins can offer a loin without blemish, not he who was a sinner. For this cause in the sacrifice of peace offerings he distinguished goats from lambs.
05_marg1888: BUT IF OF THE FLOCK etc. HESYCHIUS. Whom he commands to offer an ox, whom again a sheep, and whom a goat, we have said above. For the ox is he who works the commandments of the law; sheep, the simple; goats, because simple, formerly sinners, now penitent. But there he mingled goats with sheep, saying: And if the offering be of the flocks, of sheep or of goats etc. But the Seventy: If his gift be from the sheep, from the lambs and kids, he shall offer it without blemish. For the sheep seems to be the kind of lambs and kids. Whence Amos: I am of the peoples, and the Lord took me from the flocks of the sheep; since 'of the peoples' is properly said of one who feeds on goats. Because therefore the law speaks of some as lambs, of some as goats: and lambs are only the simple who have sinned in nothing, but goats the simple who have sinned and been converted: rightly in a manner the sacrifice in holocaust is one. For he who after sin wishes to savour perfect things ought to live as one who has not sinned before. But in the sacrifice of peace offerings, though he had kept the rest the same in sheep and goats and oxen, he set this one thing more in sheep: that he commanded to be offered not only the fat and the caul of the liver, or according to the Seventy the lobe of the liver and the kidneys, but also the rump, or also according to the Seventy, the loin without blemish with the kidneys. Rightly he calls it the soul which he describes as sinning: for he would not call the spirit that which he said would sin, nor the man, in whom, sin intervening, the image of God would not stand. The soul that sinneth etc. The lawgiver omitted nothing necessary: he assigned the differences of ways of life, and in the offering of sacrifices the ways of living; at length he sets forth the sacrifice of Christ, through which remission and redemption of sins was given to us. And it is to be noted that he said the sin was the soul's, against those who accuse the body as the cause of sin. But if the soul is free from it, the luxury of the flesh harms it nothing. Rather, if the soul rules well, it at once ceases and withdraws. But if the soul sins through ignorance, yet it is not compelled by the flesh, but by negligence and the imitation of worse things, through which it thinks harmful things useful. It is to be noted also that in many things he mingles the priest as one like the others, offering for sins: for Christ ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might become a merciful and faithful priest. But the lawgiver calls the sin of the priest the sin of the people. For the sensible priest, being negligent or sinning or not punishing, makes the people sin; but the intelligible priest in no way did sin. Yet, as far as we can, let us fit what is said to the intelligible priest. For if anyone abuses the patience of God, God seems to give him licence to sin. Whence Isaias: Why hast thou made us to err, O Lord, from thy ways? why hast thou hardened our heart etc.? Habacuc also complains of the like: Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself etc.? The lawgiver seems therefore to signify the priest to whom it was said: "Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech"; and who was anointed by the Father, according to that: "Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee." He offered himself a sacrifice for our sins. Whence Paul says: Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many. Yet he offers himself for his own sin, because he took our sin upon himself. Whence: Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin.

05_marg1918: AND IF A SOUL SHALL SIN etc. ORIGEN. Doing one of all the commandments of the Lord, which shall not be done. Long did amazement hold me astonished at this saying. For I do not see it said consistently: if a soul shall sin and do one of the commandments of the Lord, which shall not be done. For if it is a commandment of the Lord, how ought it not to have been done, since commandments are given that they may be done? Yet I see that all the translators have put it alike. It is not therefore an error of translation, but a deep sense. For some commandments of the Lord are given that they may be done, some that they may not be done; but human necessity demanded that among those which ought to be done there should be inserted those which ought not to be done. A lamb is commanded to be immolated at the Pasch, not that God required the victim of a lamb every year, but that he might mark that the lamb ought to be immolated "who taketh away the sin of the world". This therefore he willed, that he did not will. Whence: To what purpose do you offer me the multitude of your victims etc.? Yet he commanded how these things should be done. He who has offered these carnally is a soul of the people of the land, which sins unwillingly, doing one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done. And when the sin is made known to it, it brings its gift before the Lord, when it has known that God does not seek such a sacrifice; because a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit, and God desires mercy rather than sacrifice. 05_marg1935: AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether what is said is to be taken everywhere: that if his hand be not able to offer a sheep, he ought to offer a pair of turtles or two young pigeons; and if he be not able for this either, a certain quantity of fine flour. For if it is understood everywhere, it cannot be said that the priest has not a calf, or the synagogue or the prince has not a goat or a sheep. And if it is so, what need was there afterwards to say that silent perjury, or the touching of an unclean thing, and perjury done through ignorance were purged by the sacrifice of an ewe lamb or a she goat, when the same precept is in that generality to which these could have belonged? But if these are distinguished, so that it was lawful for them to offer turtles or doves, or, if these were lacking, fine flour, but where this is not said it was not lawful, it does not seem that the poor were helped, since there could be many offences not specially expressed which are referred to that generality, where the needy would be burdened if it were lawful to offer only the she goat and the ewe lamb, and not also those little birds and fine flour. Unless perhaps someone says that these expressly named are distinguished from those mentioned generally because here he said ewe lamb, there sheep, so that age makes some difference: provided only it be understood that the poor were helped, so that if they had not those four-footed beasts they might offer the said birds or fine flour for sins of ignorance. But if it troubles anyone why, when he had concluded generally all sins of ignorance, and had distinguished the sacrifices not by the difference of the sins, which he had not made, but by the difference of the persons, he afterwards would also distinguish the sins and command sacrifices according to their variety and diversity, as though all did not belong to that generality: the exception afterwards made is to be understood thus, that whatever remain, these which are specially mentioned being excepted, we understand in that generality; which manner of speech is found not only in the holy Scriptures. Such is that: "Every sin that a man doth is without the body." For he seems to have left out no sin; yet afterwards he excepts: But he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body; which according to the custom of speech would be said thus: Every sin that a man doth, fornication excepted, is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. And here, when he had first spoken generally of all those sins of ignorance which were to be expiated by the sacrifices he mentioned, afterwards he excepted those to which, set out distinctly, he would apply a certain purgation of sacrifices, so that all the rest besides these should belong to that generality.

05_marg1936: HESYCHIUS. Allegorically. It is a measure of three measures, that is, containing three bushels. Christ therefore is he who offers the sacrifice, and he himself is the sacrifice. Because the ephi, a measure of three bushels, hints at the Trinity; because it is one measure, since in it is one Godhead; but it has three measures, that is, three perfect persons and as many subsistences; so that we do not sin if we call the flesh of the Lord a part, on account of the inseparable union of the incarnate Word; for it is a part of the Trinity, because its glory and power are indivisible. Whence the Apostle: "In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally." And John: Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father. He that confesseth Jesus hath the Father also. Christ therefore is the ephi, having in himself the fulness of the Trinity: the tenth of it is his flesh, in which is shown the loftiness of his Godhead in respect of his humanity; for which reason it is also called a part; and the Word was incarnate in a whole man, who also fulfilled the law. Ten is perfect, and contains the ten commandments of the law. Whence also the law assigned to the priest, that is, to Christ, the chief tenth of the tithe, as having the firstfruits of our lump. He therefore who after transgression wishes to do penance, let him do it in the hope of Christ, who says: I say not to thee, till seven times, but till seventy times seven times. 05_marg1946: AUGUSTINE. It is asked how this offence is distinguished from those which he included generally: for to certain kinds of sins certain sacrifices of expiation seem to be applied. Then he excepts certain kinds of sins, and expressed by name what is to be offered for which: as for perjury heard and kept silent, for the touching of a carcass and of an unclean thing, and for false swearing through ignorance, an ewe lamb or a she goat or a pair of turtles or two young pigeons, or the tenth part of an ephi of fine flour. But now, no species of sin being expressed, adding generally: Any soul that shall offend, and do against any of the precepts of the Lord the things which ought not to be done (as he said in that generality): One of the precepts of the Lord which shall not be done, and shall not know it, and shall offend, that is, shall sin unwillingly through ignorance, he commands a ram to be offered, not a she goat or a female sheep, as he had appointed in such a generality of sins. What then does this mingling mean? Unless that what he says here: For he hath offended with an offence, an offence before the Lord; by this that he says, before the Lord, he wished the offence to be understood in those things which are done before the Lord, that is, by which the Lord is served in the tabernacle. 05_marg1950: ORIGEN. The soul that shall sin etc. I think that we have received our soul and body as a deposit from God; and, what is a greater deposit, he has committed to thy soul his image and likeness: this must be restored as whole as it is plain it was received from thee. If thou art merciful, as thy Father also is merciful, the image of God is in thee, and thou keepest the deposit whole; and if thou art perfect, as thy Father also is perfect, and the likenesses which are in God by nature are present to thee by imitation, the deposit of the divine image is safe with thee. If on the contrary thou art cruel, impious, violent and the like, casting away the image of God thou hast taken up the image of the devil, and hast denied the good deposit. Whence: O Timothy, keep the good deposit. I add this also, that we have received Christ as a deposit, and the Holy Ghost: we must see therefore that we do not use the holy deposit unholily, and, when sins solicit us to consent to them, swear that we have not received the deposit, which if we had, we could not consent to sin. The rational sense too which is in me is committed to me, that I may use it for the understanding of divine things. Talent, understanding, memory, judgment, reason and all the motions that are within me seem committed to me, that in them I may use them for the things which the divine Law commands. But if the talent, skilful and keen, is turned to evil arts, and abuses the things of God in what he does not will, this is to forswear the deposit and turn benefits into faithlessness. There are robbers good and evil. Good, who take the kingdom of God by force; evil, of whom it is said: The spoil of the poor is in your house. Whence: extortioners shall not possess the kingdom of God. Some also, according to spiritual understanding, seize blameworthily, as others seize the kingdom of heaven praiseworthily. If anyone not yet purged of vices, nor yet separated from filthy acts, wishes to thrust himself secretly into the company of the saints and hear the discourse in which perfect and mystic things are treated, he has not rightly seized the knowledge of the secret and perfect things. For no one putteth new wine into old bottles.

05_marg1957: AND THE PRIEST SHALL FEED IT etc. Allegorically. In the morning Christ was judged, in the evening crucified. Fire therefore is put under morning and evening, because the charity of God is nourished in us while we recall Christ judged in the morning and crucified in the evening.
05_marg1958: GREGORY. Tropologically. The altar of God is our heart, on which fire is commanded always to burn, because it is necessary that the flame of charity ascend from it unceasingly. To it the priest puts wood, lest it be put out: namely any preacher of Christ, a member of the supreme priest; and each of the faithful ceases not to gather in his heart the examples of the saints and the testimonies of Scripture; with these we ought to nourish and stir up the fire if perchance it languishes. Wood is put under in the morning when the night of blindness is put out. Or, because the morning is the first part of the day, let each of the faithful, putting earthly thoughts aside, think on this in the beginning. And laying on the holocaust, he shall burn thereupon the fat of the peace offerings. For whoever kindles this fire of charity in himself lays himself upon it as a holocaust, and burns up every vice which lived wickedly in him. For then he considers his inward parts, and slays his reprobate life with the sword of immolation, when he has laid himself upon the altar of his heart and kindled himself with the fire of charity. Of the victim of peace offerings he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings, because the fattening of the new life makes peace between us and God and renders a most sweet odour. And because the same charity remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is well added: This is the perpetual fire etc. This fire fails not from the altar, because in the future the fervour of charity increases in the minds of the saints. For by eternal contemplation it comes about that the more God is seen, the more he is loved.
05_marg1959: AND LAYING ON THE HOLOCAUST etc. AUGUSTINE. We must see whether no day was passed over on which a holocaust and the saving fat were not found; or whether it was not laid on except in the morning, on whatever day it was laid on. For if we understand it daily, what if no one offered? But if the priest provided the daily holocausts as from the public store or from his own, upon them were laid the things which the Lord commanded, offered by the people for sins, to be laid upon the holocausts; and it was not necessary for one offering a sacrifice for sin to offer a holocaust also on which it might be laid, except where a pair of turtles or two young pigeons are offered. For there he determines that one be offered for sin and the other for a holocaust, and first for sin, then for a holocaust. It is asked also whether the holocaust which he commanded to be laid on in the morning burned through the whole night until the next morning; or whether, since he says it ought to burn all night, the holocaust is the evening one, and he began from that to speak of the law of the holocaust, so as to begin from the evening holocaust; which is strange if he kept silent and did not admonish that such things were offered in the evening.

05_marg1974: WHICH IN A FRYINGPAN etc. GREGORY. Morally. No sacrifice is such to God as zeal for souls. Whence: "The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up." Therefore the fine flour tempered with oil is fried in a fryingpan. For the priest who succeeds his father offers it hot for a most sweet odour to the Lord. The fine flour is fried with oil in the fryingpan when the clean mind of the just is burned through the zeal of a holy odour. And it is commanded to be tempered with oil, because in Greek eleos is called mercy, which burns and shines in the sight of God. Let the strictness of holy zeal therefore burn and grow bright with the virtue of mercy. For it loves even what it pursues. Whence it is offered hot for a most sweet odour to the Lord. For if zeal has not love, the fine flour in the fryingpan has lost its heat. The priest who succeeds his father offers it, he namely who shows himself a son of God by his conduct and does not fall away from his nobility. It is wholly burned on the altar, that it may become a holocaust. A holocaust is wholly burnt, and every holocaust is a sacrifice, but not conversely. There are many good things done that are sacrifices but not holocausts. For those who so work the things that are of God that they do not leave the things that are of the world offer a sacrifice, not a holocaust. But those who forsake all things that are of the world, and with their whole mind are kindled with the fire of divine love, become a sacrifice and a holocaust to God. The fine flour in the fryingpan therefore is the mind of the just, which in the affliction of spiritual zeal is fried through solicitude for souls, and is reckoned to God as a holocaust.

05_marg1978: THE PRIEST THAT OFFERETH SHALL EAT IT etc. AUGUSTINE. Not what he lays on, for that is consumed by fire, but what remains of it. But he says afterwards: All the things that are for sin, of whose blood something has been brought into the tabernacle of the testimony to make atonement in the holy place, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. How then do the remains of the sacrifices for sins belong to the priests to be eaten? Wherefore it is to be understood that those are excepted with whose blood the altar of incense is touched. For this he commanded to be done of the calf which the priest offers for his own sin, and of the calf for the sin of the synagogue, that the flesh which remained should be burned outside the camp: this too he now briefly recalls.
05_marg1979: ORIGEN. Some of the victims are God's alone; some are Aaron's and his sons'; some his and his sons' and his daughters', so that it is lawful for the priest's wife also to eat. Of these some are the priests' and their sons' and daughters', but of which it is lawful for the children of Israel also to eat. And in those of which it is lawful for the children of Israel to eat, the priests and their sons have a share; yet it is not lawful for the children of Israel to eat of every victim of which the priest eats. The first victim therefore is the holocaust. For the first ought to be none but that which is offered to almighty God. The second is that which is eaten by the priests. The third, that of which the children of Israel may eat, namely the clean only. For only the clean are commanded to eat of the sacrifices. Mystically seek these victims within thyself, having within thyself herds of oxen, which are blessed in Abraham, and flocks of sheep and goats, in which the patriarchs were blessed and multiplied. There are within thee also the birds of heaven. Do not wonder: understand that thou art another world, and that within thyself are the sun and moon and stars. Whence it is said to Abraham: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst, for their multitude. So shall thy seed be as the stars of heaven: namely those who, begotten of his faith, live rationally and keep the divine laws and precepts. The Saviour also says: "You are the light of the world." Doubt not therefore that the sun and moon are within thee; hear something greater, lest thou neglect thy life as cheap. This world has its governor, who dwells in it, almighty God. Whence he says: Do not I fill heaven and earth? Hear what the Almighty says of men: I will dwell in them, and walk among them. He adds something more concerning thy person: I will be a Father to them, and they shall be my sons and daughters. Where the holocaust is slain, which is offered to God alone, there also is the victim for sin; that namely he who has sinned and repents, and offers the victim of a contrite spirit, may understand that he stands in a holy place and is joined to the things that pertain to God. He offers before the Lord, or in the sight of the Lord, who does not go out from the sight of the Lord, as Cain, but stands confidently, nor does he turn from his gaze through the consciousness of sin. Therefore he says this victim is holy of holies. Hear something greater. What is the victim which is offered for sins and is holy of holies, but the Only-begotten of God, my Lord Jesus Christ? He is the victim for sins and the holy of holies. The priest that offereth it shall eat it. This is the priest who eats and consumes the sins of the people, who is a priest for ever. And our God is a consuming fire, namely of human sins. Those he consumes, those he devours, those he purges. Whence elsewhere he says: And I will purge thee with fire to purity. For he took our sins upon himself, and in himself ate them up as fire. The priest that hath offered it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle. For it follows that, according to him who gave the priesthood to the Church, the priests of the Church should take on the sins of the people and, imitating the master, grant remission of sins. Who ought to be so perfect and so learned in their offices that in a holy place, by not sinning themselves, they may consume the sins of the people. Moses had come into a holy place, to whom it was said: The place whereon thou standest is holy ground. And in the Church the place is made faith, charity, a good conscience. The priest shall eat the flesh of the sacrifice in the court of the tabernacle of the testimony when he can understand what is the reason or what the mysteries in the things that are written of the courts of the tabernacle of the testimony: to which no one draws near, which are open to none but the priests, who by knowledge and mystic understanding can penetrate their secrets. There are other more secret doctrines in the Church, which it is not lawful even for the priests to approach, namely where the ark is laid up and the pot and the tables of the testament, but only for the one high priest, and for him once a year, at fixed times and with mystic purifications. There are others to which the Levites also can come. There are others too which the children of Israel can approach, that is, the laity, yet not foreigners, unless they have already been enrolled in the Church of the Lord. For the Egyptian shall enter into the Church of God in the third generation, that is, in the faith of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, by which everyone believes who is joined to the Church of God. But it is to be known that, although some of the victims are granted to the priests to eat, yet not all. For some part is offered to God and given to the fires of the altar; because if it is granted us to know some things from the Scriptures, yet some are reserved to God, which surpass our senses; lest they be brought forth by us otherwise than the truth holds, we do better to reserve these to the fire.

05_marg1993: WHETHER TEMPERED WITH OIL etc. ORIGEN. The saving sacrifice is commanded to be made in oil. Upon the sacrifice for sin oil is not put, because it is for sin. Therefore it has neither the oil of gladness nor the frankincense of sweetness. For mourning befits sinners, not gladness or the odour of sweetness; because it is said in the person of the sinner: My sores are putrified and corrupted, because of my foolishness. The heart of man is an oven, which, if vices or the devil have kindled it, will not bake but burn up. But if he has kindled it who came to cast fire on the earth, it does not burn up the loaves of the Scriptures to perdition, but bakes them for sacrifice. Perhaps those things are said to be baked in the oven which are well hidden and cannot easily be brought forth to the crowd. For there are many such things which, if they are not baked in the oven, are raw and cannot be eaten, as in the vision of Ezechiel. For it is not to be believed that there is a living creature in the form of a lion, or of a calf or of an eagle, by which God is carried. There are three things in which sacrifices are prepared: in the oven, in the fryingpan, on the gridiron. The oven, according to its form, signifies the deeper things in the divine Scriptures; the fryingpan, those things which, if often turned over, can be understood and explained; the gridiron, those that are open. For there is in the divine Scriptures history, morality, the mystic sense, as body and soul and spirit. This too the basket of perfection signifies, in which three loaves are commanded to be had. For in the divine Scripture foods are set before the hearers in three ways. In the Gospel also it is said: Friend, lend me three loaves. One is baked in the oven, another in the fryingpan, the third on the gridiron.
05_marg1994: HESYCHIUS. He speaks of a sacrifice of fine flour tempered with oil which is put neither in the oven nor in the fryingpan nor on the gridiron: this is theology which is not referred to the humanity of Christ, but concerns the Father or the Holy Ghost, or the Son himself according to the Godhead. Therefore he assigned this to the sons of Aaron, who advance to theology through meditation on the Scriptures, equally, that all may think the same of God. This sacrifice the heretics do not taste, since they savour divers things. There is a sacrifice of fine flour not tempered with oil, when the tenth part of an ephi without oil and frankincense is offered for sin, namely by those who cannot offer a buck goat or a sheep or turtles or doves. This, even if it signifies the sacrifice of the Saviour, he assigned to the sons of Aaron as commanded not for the sake of theology but for the profit of the offerer.

05_marg2005: THE FLESH THAT etc. ORIGEN. The holy flesh is understood as the divine words. 05_marg2012: ORIGEN. The sacrifice which is called saving only one who is whole and conscious of his salvation offers in thanks to the Lord: one sick in mind, one languid in works, cannot offer it. That leper of the Gospel could not offer until he was cured; but when he was cleansed by the Lord, he was commanded to offer the gifts at the altar which Moses commanded for a testimony to them. The clean therefore can offer. But how shall his hands offer the victims to the Lord? Not 'the man', but 'the hands', that is, his works. For these commend the victim to the Lord. For if thy hand is closed to giving, thou art still a leper and canst not offer. Where we have victim, the Greeks have holocarpomata, which signifies 'all the fruit', which the unfruitful cannot offer, who bears not the fruit of justice and mercy and the like. And as to what he says: The fat which is upon the breast, understand the breast as the heart, from which all evil thoughts are to be taken away (for thence they proceed), that the clean heart may see God. He commanded the lobe of the liver also to be offered, in which is wrath or greed. He offers the lobe of the liver who cuts off wrath and fury from himself. The fat which is upon the breast is laid on the altar; the breast to Aaron and his sons; the right shoulder he commanded to be separated. Of what sort is the breast of the priest, full of wisdom and divine understanding; of what sort too the shoulder which the children of Israel offer to him for their salvation. These are forms which are not performed in the Church, but read. For they would not be read unless edification were offered to the hearers from them. If therefore the priest through doctrine, through much solicitude, and through the labour of watchings has converted a sinner and taught him to follow better things; if, I say, he has done such a work, he who is saved by his labour ought to give thanks to God and offer the victim of the saving offering, because he has obtained salvation. And he says the breast of laying on and the shoulder of taking off. For when all grossness has been taken from thy heart, and it has been cleansed from every covering, which is to be given to the fire, it remains that the grace of the Holy Ghost be laid upon it, and then it will become the breast of laying on. And the shoulder will be of separation. If thou knowest how to discern what are the works of light and of darkness, if thou hast separated thy works from darkness, that they may be in the light, thy shoulder is made one of separation. Or when thou hast separated thyself from every brother walking disorderly. Or when they who bear the vessels of the Lord have gone out from the midst of sinners.

05_marg2013: JEROME. TO FABIOLA. Which is upon the breast and the lobe of the liver etc. Of the saving victims the priests offer the fat, and receive the breast and the right shoulder for food. Sense is in the heart, the heart in the breast; pleasure, according to the natural philosophers, is in the liver; whence Pliny: the lobe set against pleasure, and pleasure bursting out through the windows of the eyes. After therefore they have made a fat holocaust, and burned the concupiscence of lust with the fire of the Holy Ghost, they receive the breast and the shoulder as a reward: in the breast, clean thoughts, the knowledge of the law; in the shoulder, good working and the fight against the devil, and the armed hand, that what they have conceived in mind they may prove in work. For Jesus began to do and to teach. The breast also is called addition, or chief, or excellent. "For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge" etc. This ought to be chief, and by the addition of spiritual grace he forms such a man as can resist the gainsayers and have nothing of left-handed work in himself. Let the shoulder be right and separated, that the works of the priest may be separated from all by comparison of virtues. The other three, besides the firstfruits of the victims, which are given to the priest from the private and the public shambles, where not religion but the force of necessity is: the shoulder, of which we have already spoken, the jaw and the belly. The jaw signifies the eloquent and learned man, that what he conceives in the breast he may set forth with the mouth. The belly, the receptacle of foods, pierced through with the priestly dagger in the Madianite harlot, condemns all the labours and momentary allurements of gluttony by the end of dung, showing to minds consecrated to God that all we devour is cast out into the privy. Whence: Meat for the belly, and the belly for the meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. The dust of the calf which the children of Israel worshipped he receives as drink in contempt of superstition, that he may learn to despise what he sees himself cast into the privy.

For what he says: This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord, goes back to what was above; that thou mayest know that if anyone keeps them, he will come to that dignity of the priest, and not otherwise. Whence he adds: In the day when Moses offered them, that they might do the office of priesthood, and the things which he commanded to be given them by the children of Israel. 05_marg2019: ORIGEN. When the lawgiver had set forth: This is the anointing of Aaron and of his sons etc., he did not add what it was, nor explain how he anointed; but this indeed he does in what follows. But now, after he said: This is the anointing of Aaron, he adds nothing of the anointing, that he might show that these things which he had said above, namely the breast of laying on and the shoulder of separation, are the very anointing of Aaron and his sons; lest we should think those things said of flesh, that he might teach that they too were set under the sacrament of anointing. Afterwards he repeats what he had set out above, saying: "This is the law of holocaust" etc. This is what was set out above, and it seems to be a recapitulation of the sacraments which were narrated above, as also that, namely: This is the anointing, is a foretaste of what follows: for in passing he touches on other things both to be said and already said; to be said, there: This is the anointing; said, there: "This is the law."

That high priest whom Moses then ordained knew that circumcision was spiritual; yet he kept that of the flesh also, because he could not be uncircumcised; he had therefore two tunics, one of the carnal mystery, the other of spiritual understanding.
