05_marg2024: AND WHEN HE HAD WASHED THEM etc. JEROME. Even then the sacraments of baptism signified the cleansing of the world and the holiness of all things. They do not receive the vestments unless washed, nor are they adorned for sacred things unless they are born again new men in Christ. For new wine is put into new bottles. Moses washes, that is, the law. Whence: "They have Moses and the prophets: let them hear them." From Adam to Moses all sinned. We are washed by the precepts of God, and, made ready for the coming of Christ, we lay aside the garments of skins, that we may put on the linen garment, having nothing of death in it, but wholly white; that, rising from baptism, we may gird our loins in truth, and all the foulness of our former sins may be covered. Whence: "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." After the breeches and the linen tunic we are clothed with the violet garment, ascending from earth to the heights. This is the undertunic, according to the Seventy, which signifies that the reason of lofty things is open only to the greater and perfect. This the Prophets had, Moses and Aaron and all to whom it is said: Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion. The first washing of sins, the grace of baptism, the more secret doctrine, do not suffice unless we have works, that is, the ephod, which is joined to the rational, that it be not loose nor slack. For reason needs works and works need reason, that what we conceive in mind we may accomplish in work.
05_marg2025: ORIGEN. Let Moses wash thee, that is, the law, which washes thee and rinses away thy filth. The law consecrates priests. He cannot be a priest whom the law has not appointed. If thou hast been washed by Moses, thou canst come to the vestments which Moses brings forth. But for the priestly insignia not only vestments are needed, but girdles also. Adam and his wife were clothed with garments of skins: with such it was fitting that the sinner be clothed, which were tokens of the mortality which he had contracted by sinning, and of the frailty which came from the corruption of the flesh. But if thou hast been cleansed of these by the law of the Lord, Moses will clothe thee with the garment of incorruption, that thy shame may nowhere appear, and this mortal may be swallowed up by life. 05_marg2026: JEROME. TO FABIOLA. Let us learn first the common vestments of the priests and of the high priests. 05_marg2027: JEROME. The second is the poderis of linen, that is, a garment to the ankles of double fine cloth, which Josephus calls of byssus: this clings to the body, so close and with tight sleeves that there is no wrinkle in the garment, and it comes down to the legs. Soldiers are wont to have such linen shirts, which they call camisiae, fitted and bound to the limbs, that they may be unencumbered for everything. This tunic the priests use, having the beauty of the clothed and the quickness of the naked; and it is called the linen one.
05_marg2028: The third is the girdle, most like the skin of a serpent which it casts off in summer, so woven in the round like a long purse, under a weft of scarlet, purple and violet and fine linen, for beauty and strength, so distinguished with many-coloured work that you would think the divers flowers and gems not woven but added by the craftsman's hand. With this belt the linen tunic is bound between the navel and the breast; it has a breadth of four fingers and, coming down in great part to the legs, when there is need of quickness for the sacrifices it is thrown back over the left shoulder.
05_marg2029: THE SAME. The fourth is a round cap, which the Greeks and our people call tiara, some galerus. It has no point at the top, nor does it cover the whole head down to the hair, but leaves a third part bare from the forehead; it is bound with a band lest it slip; it is of byssus, and so skilfully covered with a linen cloth that there are no traces of the needle outside. These four both the priests and the high priests use. The remaining four belong properly to the high priests. The first of which, and here the fifth, is the tunic to the ankles, wholly violet, having sleeves of the same colour sewn on; the opening by which it is put on, which is commonly called the capitium, has very firm borders lest it tear. And in the lower part are seventy-two bells and as many pomegranates, woven of the same colours as the girdle; between two bells one pomegranate, and between two pomegranates one bell; that when the high priest goes into the Holy of Holies he may be all sounding: if he did not do this, he would die at once.
05_marg2030: The sixth in Hebrew is ephod, that is, the superhumeral: for wherever in Exodus or Leviticus the superhumeral is read, in the Hebrew it is ephod. Samuel, however, a Levite still of tender age, and David before the ark, wore an ephod. But one is woven of violet, fine linen, scarlet, purple and gold; another, in the likeness of the priests, simple and of linen. Plates of gold, that is, leaves, are beaten out to a wonderful thinness, from which threads are cut and twisted, with the weft of three colours, violet, scarlet, purple, and the warp of fine linen; whence is made a little mantle of embroidered beauty and wonderful brightness, in the manner of the caracallae, but without hoods. Over the breast nothing is woven; a place is left for the rational. On each shoulder single stones are set, bound in gold, which in Hebrew are called soom, by Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion onyx stones, by the Seventy emeralds. Josephus calls them sardius stones, agreeing with the Hebrew, so as to show either the colour of the stones or their country. On each are six names of the Patriarchs, by whom the Israelite people is divided: on the right shoulder the elder sons of Jacob, on the left the younger; that the high priest, going into the Holy of Holies, may carry on his shoulders the people for whom he is to pray.
05_marg2031: The seventh is small, but the most holy of all: in Hebrew it is called hosen, in Greek logion, in Latin rationale. It is a short cloth woven of gold and the four colours of which the superhumeral also is made, having the size of a palm in the square, doubled, lest it tear. In it are set twelve stones of wonderful size and price in four rows, three stones in each line. In the first, sardius, topaz, emerald; in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper; in the third, ligure, which perhaps is also hyacinth, agate and amethyst; in the fourth, chrysolite, onyx, beryl. On each are written the names of the twelve tribes according to their ages. Of these stones the heavenly Jerusalem is built in the Apocalypse: by their names or appearance the order or diversity of the virtues is indicated. At the four corners of the rational are four rings of gold, having opposite them on the superhumeral four others, so that ring comes against ring, and they are joined to each other with violet bands. And lest the size and weight of the stones break the threads, they are bound and enclosed in gold. Chains also are made of gold, which for beauty are covered with little golden pipes, and have on the rational above two larger rings, which are fastened with golden hooks of the superhumeral, and below two others. For behind, on the superhumeral, against the breast and stomach, on each side were rings of gold, which were joined with the golden rings of the rational, so that the rational was joined to the superhumeral and to beholders was thought one woven work.
05_marg2032: The eighth is the plate of gold, on which is written the name of the Lord in four Hebrew letters, Yod, He, Vau, He, which among them is called ineffable. This is added in the high priest over the linen cap common to all the priests, that it may be bound on the forehead with a violet band, and the name of God may crown and protect all the beauty of the high priest.
05_marg2033: And the pomegranates and bells set in the lower parts show lightnings and thunders, or earth and water and all the elements sounding together with one another, and so interwoven with each other that all are in each.
05_marg2034: JEROME. The Hebrews refer the four colours to the four elements, of which all things subsist. Fine linen they assign to the earth, because it is produced from the earth; purple to the sea, because it is dyed with its shellfish; violet to the air, for the likeness of colour; scarlet, which in Hebrew is thola, that is, the little worm, to fire and the ether. For they recall that this was done so that the high priest might pray to the Creator not only for Israel but for the whole world, which consists of earth and water and air and fire: for these are the elements of all things. Whence the first vestment is of linen, signifying earth; the second violet, showing the air, which is raised little by little from earthly things to the heights; and the violet vestment reaching from the head to the ankles indicates the air poured from the heavens to the earth. That the said colours are woven with gold they wish to figure this: that the vital heat and the providence of the divine mind penetrate all things.
05_marg2035: ORIGEN. In Exodus, where the priestly vestments are commanded, I find there are eight kinds which are prepared for the high priest; but here only seven: for the eighth is left out, which is the girdle-cloth, or, as we read elsewhere, the linen breeches. But perhaps because in this kind of garment, by which the thighs are covered or the loins bound, there is a token of chastity, those parts were not always bound in those priests. For sometimes indulgence is given for the posterity of the race. But in the priests of the Church I see another sacrament. For they can beget sons in the Church. Whence: "My little children, of whom I am in labour again" etc. And elsewhere: For in Christ Jesus, by the gospel, I have begotten you. In such generations they sometimes use the breeches and abstain, when they see that they cannot have fruit in their hearers, in whom the seed would perish and make no offspring. When therefore they see them incapable, or feigned and hypocrites, they put on the girdle-cloth, they use the breeches, lest that which is holy be given to dogs, and pearls be cast before swine.

Without bells, divers colours, gems and the flowers of the virtues he neither enters the Church nor is high priest.

05_marg2039: JEROME. THE SUPERHUMERAL. The superhumeral and the two emerald or onyx stones which cover the shoulders above they interpret as the two hemispheres, of which one is above the earth and the other below the earth; or the sun and moon which shine above.
05_marg2040: The two stones on the superhumeral are Christ and the Church, containing the names of the twelve apostles who were sent to preach. Or the letter and the spirit, in which are all the mysteries of the law: on the right the spirit, on the left the letter. Through letters we come to words, through words to sense. A beautiful order, signifying sacraments by the very habit: in the shoulders works, in the breast reason. Whence also the priests eat the breast.

05_marg2041: AND BINDING IT WITH THE GIRDLE etc. ORIGEN. He girded him according to the making of the superhumeral. He had already said above: He girded him with a girdle over the tunic. What is that double girdle? Let him be bound in word, unencumbered for all things in work; let him have nothing slack, nothing loose. Let him be girded with the virtues of the mind, bound from bodily vices; let him fear no lapse of the soul, none of the body: let him always use both girdles, that he may be holy in body and spirit. He is girded according to the making of the superhumeral, because he uses the girdle of virtue according to his works.

05_marg2042: HE FITTED THE RATIONAL etc. JEROME. The rational, set in the middle, indicates the earth, which, like a point, though it has all things in itself, is walled about by all the elements.
05_marg2043: ORIGEN. He put upon him the logion, which is the rational, and upon the logion manifestation and truth. It does not suffice the high priest to have wisdom and to know the reason of all things unless he can manifest to the people what he knows. Therefore manifestation is laid upon the rational, that he may be able to answer everyone that asks him a reason of the faith and truth. Truth also is laid on, that he may not build up what he has thought out by his own wit, but what the truth holds. Another adornment is to be added, whence it is necessary that he receive a crown: he receives therefore the cidaris, which is the covering or adornment of the head. After this the mitre is put on before the face, that is, at the forehead of the high priest, the sanctified plate of gold on which the name of God is graven. But this adornment of the head, in which the name of God is set, is put on after those things by which the lower members of the body had been adorned. For above all things that can be perceived or understood of the world or of creatures, the knowledge of God excels as of the author of all things. And because he is the head of all, therefore this adornment is put upon the head above all: for nothing is added to the head of the high priest after these.
05_marg2044: JEROME. The rational is twofold, open and hidden, simple and mystic; it has twelve stones and four rows, that is, four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice, which cling to each other; and while they are mingled together they make twelve. Or the four Gospels, full of eyes and enlightening the world: in one, four, and in four, each. Whence doctrine and truth are in the breast of the priest. When one is wrapped in a manifold garment, it follows that he should bring forth in speech the truth which he holds in heart. Therefore the rational is also truth, that is, it is knowledge, that he may know what is to be taught; and manifestation and doctrine, that he may manifest what he has conceived in mind. First the superhumeral, after it the rational. Whence: "By thy commandments I have had understanding." First we do, then we teach, lest doctrine be destroyed by empty works. Sow for yourselves in justice, reap the fruit of life, enlighten yourselves with knowledge. First one must sow, and afterwards reap the fruit, that we may claim knowledge for ourselves. Nor does this suffice unless reason cleave to works and works to reason, and, these going before, doctrine and truth follow.
05_marg2045: THE SAME. The twelve stones are either the zodiac circle or the twelve months, and in each row the several seasons, and three months each. And beautifully what is in the middle is called the rational. For all things are full of reason, and earthly things cling to heavenly. Rather the reason of earthly things and of seasons, of heat and cold, and the twofold temperateness between both, comes down from the course and reason of heaven. Whence the rational is bound with the ephod. In the rational is manifestation and doctrine, or truth, because in the reason of God there is never a lie, and truth itself is shown by many signs and proofs. Whence it came about that we should know the reason of the sun and moon, of the year, the months and seasons and hours, of storms, fair weather and winds, and of all things, receiving the wisdom implanted by God, he himself, the dweller and teacher, showing us the knowledge of his dwelling and his workmanship.

05_marg2046: HE PUT THE PLATE etc. JEROME. The learning of all things profits nothing unless it be crowned by the knowledge of God, which is ever with him and the Father. Whence he put the plate upon the cidaris.
05_marg2047: JEROME. All things are imperfect unless a driver be sought for the chariot, and the Creator, standing over the creatures, himself rule what he made. What was once shown in the plate is now shown in the sign of the cross: the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the law. Then, according to Ezechiel, the sign thau was fixed on the forehead of those that sigh; now, bearing the cross, we say: "The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us" etc.
05_marg2048: The plate of gold on the forehead of the high priest and the name inscribed signify that all things that are upon the earth are governed by the will of God. For it was just that the high priest of God, bearing the type of all creatures in his vestments, should show that all things need the mercy of God; and that when he sacrificed, the whole condition of things should be expiated, where he prayed by voice and habit not for children, parents and kin, but for every creature.
05_marg2049: HE TOOK ALSO THE OIL OF UNCTION etc. He is the Son of God who anoints and who is anointed: anointing by the word of the Godhead, according to which he has all things in common with the Father and the Holy Ghost. He is anointed by the Father, according to that: "God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness" etc. The Holy Ghost anointed him, according to Isaias: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me etc. And what the Father and the Holy Ghost do, these the Son also does. He anoints therefore according to the Godhead, he is anointed according to the humanity. Whence Daniel too sees him offered, but does not see one offering, because he offers himself. Moses therefore anointed and offers, bearing the figure of Christ.
05_marg2050: SANCTIFYING etc. ORIGEN. It signifies the heavenly creation enriched by our sanctification, that is, through the Lord's flesh taken from us. Whence: That the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers through the church etc.

05_marg2051: POURING IT UPON THE HEAD etc. The head of Christ is the Godhead. For as the head is not divided from the feet, so neither the Godhead of Christ from his humanity after the anointing. Whence he says: "God, thy God, hath anointed thee" etc. For so God is anointed and sanctified.
05_marg2052: HIS SONS ALSO etc. ORIGEN. Mark the difference of the lesser priests from the greater. To these are not given the double vestments, nor the superhumeral, nor the rational, nor the adornment of the head, but only the cidaris and the girdle which binds only the tunic. They receive therefore the grace of the priesthood and perform the office, but not as he who is adorned with the superhumeral and the rational, who shines with manifestation and truth, who is graced with the ornament of the golden plate. I think therefore that it is one thing in priests to perform the office, another to be furnished and adorned in conduct. For anyone can perform the solemn ministry to the people, but few are they who, adorned in conduct, doctrine and wisdom, are fit to manifest the truth, and who bring forth the knowledge of the faith not without the ornament of understanding and the brightness of assertions, which the adornment of the golden plate set on the head designates. One therefore is the name of the priesthood, but not one the dignity according to the merit of life or the virtues of the soul. In these things therefore which the divine law says, let each priest look at himself as in a mirror; if he sees himself adorned in all the things said above, and such and so great in knowledge and in acts or in doctrine, let him know that he holds the high priesthood not only in name but in merit. Otherwise let him know that a lower rank is set for him, even if he has received the name of the first.

05_marg2054: HE OFFERED ALSO THE CALF etc. HESYCHIUS. What the force of this law is, how it is taken in the sacrifice of Christ, has been set out above. 05_marg2055: AUGUSTINE. When he mentioned the sacrifices for sins, he said a calf was to be offered for the sin of the priest who made the people sin; but afterwards, when it is said how the things which the Lord commanded were done toward Aaron and his sons, a calf is said to be offered for sin. But above he commanded the horns of the altar of incense to be touched with the blood of the calf, and some of the blood to be sprinkled before the veil, and the rest poured at the base of the altar of holocausts; but afterwards, when Aaron is sanctified, nothing is said of the sprinkling of the blood before the veil; of the horns of the altar it is said, but 'of incense' is not added; and it is added that the blood is to be poured at the base of the altar, nor is it said at the base of which, as though it must necessarily be taken of that whose horns were touched with blood. Since therefore it is set down ambiguously, one is free to understand it done as had been commanded of the calf for sin: that we understand the horns touched to be not of the altar at whose base its blood was poured, but of the altar of incense, and the blood poured at the base of the altar of sacrifices.

05_marg2056: HE OFFERED ALSO A RAM etc. HESYCHIUS. The law, having the priest figure Christ in many things, now commands him to immolate a calf for sins and burn it outside the camp. For so the sacrifice of Christ was made for the washing away of our sins. But now a ram for a holocaust, because the world is crucified to him, and the way of life that renounces the world, which is the holocaust, has Christ for teacher and example; because of which he says: He that taketh not up his cross and followeth me is not worthy of me, that is: he who does not so renounce the world as I teach (for this is to follow him) is not worthy of me. Why then is the holocaust divided, and its feet and entrails, or according to others the belly, washed? The interpretation of the holocaust made at the beginning of the book has sufficiently fulfilled this. There he said the parts of the offerings were made, signifying that body and soul ought to be offered. But these divisions too are in us, because the flesh lusteth against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; but not in Christ. Therefore the law made no mention of division in that sacrifice. And the priest offers a calf for sin, a ram for a holocaust, by which it is signified that the perfect way of life, which is the holocaust, is offered in the ram. For this one gives leadership to the sheep going in and going out, as Christ is the leader of the perfect way of life; and therefore he commanded the sheep to go in and out through him.

05_marg2065: AND THE RIGHT SHOULDER etc. GREGORY. The priest by the precept of the law is commanded to receive the right and separated shoulder, that his working may be not only useful but also singular; nor may he do right things only among the wicked, but may surpass those subject to him who work well, as in the honour of rank, so in the virtue of conduct. To him the breast also is given with the shoulder, that what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice he may learn to immolate of himself; that he may not only think in the breast the things that are right, but may invite the beholders to lofty things by the shoulder of work. Let him seek no prosperity of the present life and fear no adversity; let him despise the allurements of the world in regard of inward terror, and scorn its terrors, considering the allurement of inward sweetness; which Moses also says in what follows.

05_marg2066: AND HE TOOK THE BREAST etc. AUGUSTINE. Above, because he was commanding generally, if the priest had sinned, he commanded the priest himself, anointed and consecrated, that is, the high priest, to offer these things; but now Moses offers and receives the breast of laying on, because the fat was laid on from it, as he mentioned of the saving sacrifice. Since then the high priesthood seems to have begun from Aaron, but Moses was not a priest, how did he do these things? But if he was, how did the high priesthood begin from Aaron? Yet the Psalm in which it is said: "Moses and Aaron among his priests" affirms that he was a priest. Yet Aaron is commanded to receive the priestly vestment, which contains a great sacrament, and his successors, before anything is commanded about sanctifying and ordaining the priests; when, Moses going up into the mount, the priests are commanded not to go up, that is, the sons of Aaron, not because they already were, but because they were to be. Were both therefore then high priests, Moses and Aaron, or rather Moses, and Aaron under him? Or was the latter also high because of the pontifical vestment, the former because of a more excellent ministry? For from the beginning it is said: He shall be to thee in the things that pertain to the people, thou to him in the things that pertain to God.

05_marg2067: HE SPRINKLED UPON THE ALTAR etc. Whatever good things are in us are to be brought back to him as our head. Whence: "For them do I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth." Plainly therefore he called his passion sanctification, which sanctification is given to us.
05_marg2068: AND TAKING THE OINTMENT etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked who anointed the priest after the death of Moses, who succeeded only one who had died. Was it one who was already anointed among the second priests? For the oil of the high and the second priest was the same. Only that high priest whose supremacy appeared took the vestment; and if so, did he take it himself, or did another clothe him, as after the death of Aaron Moses clothed his brother's son? If then he was clothed by him, was the high one clothed by a second? For the vestment was such that it had to be put on by another; or was it put on the first time as afterwards? For sometimes he laid it aside and took it up again. A second therefore could clothe the first, by serving, not by excelling.

05_marg2081: AUGUSTINE. Take ye one he goat of the goats for sin, and a ram and a calf and a lamb of a year for a holocarposis without blemish, and a calf of the oxen, and a ram for a sacrifice of the saving offering before the Lord, and fine flour tempered with oil, because today the Lord will be seen in you. Four kinds of sacrifices of animals he commended above: the holocaust, the one for sin, the saving one, and the one of completion; but the sacrifice of completion pertains to the sanctification of the priest; the other three are here commanded to be offered. And this is said to the elders of Israel, that they may pertain to the whole people. But the sacrifice for sin has here three beasts: the he goat, the ram and the calf. To the holocaust belongs the lamb; to the saving sacrifice, the calf and the ram. It is not therefore to be distinguished so that only the he goat is understood for sin, and three in holocaust, ram, calf and lamb; but rather the first three for sin, he goat, ram, calf, and the lamb in holocaust; because above he commanded a he goat to be offered for the sin of the prince, and for each one's own sin, when he sins before the Lord by doing one of the things which ought not to be done, a ram; for the sin of the whole Synagogue a calf. It is fitting therefore that when he speaks to the senate of what the whole people ought to offer, a he goat should be commanded for the princes, and a ram for each one's own sin, and a calf for the sin of the whole Synagogue, which namely is done by the common will of all. And in the saving sacrifice he commands a calf and a ram to be offered, which are the chief. But in giving precepts about the saving sacrifices he commanded them to be offered from wherever, whether male or female, provided only they were offered of none but sheep and goats. If it is asked why he commanded two, the calf and the ram, it is hard to find, unless perhaps he willed the calf to be the saving sacrifice of the whole people, the ram for each one as for individuals. He seems above to have commanded two kinds of saving sacrifice: one which he called the saving sacrifice as in the name of all; the other where he said: If anyone offer the sacrifice of his saving offering. Where we find a difference, because in that which he called saving he did not say that the fat of the breast was to be offered to the Lord and the breast also and the right shoulder given to the priest, as in that which he called of his saving offering; because he offered the saving sacrifice for the whole people. It is not yet 'of his saving offering', which perhaps is understood as the private one of individuals, not the public one of all. For Moses offered the saving sacrifice, and it is not said 'of his saving offering', because he offered for the whole people. And where all are, there also are individuals, but not conversely.

For he did not command them to abstain from wine altogether, but when we go up to the tabernacle of the testimony or to the altar, that is, when we touch the mystery of heavenly doctrine; of which the altar is a figure, as the tabernacle is of the handling of heavenly things. Whence Paul to Timothy: Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thy frequent infirmities. And he who uses a little abstains from much wine and drunkenness at the time of the mystery and of doctrine. The priests also keep the same. Whence this commandment is delivered to the sons of Aaron too, that is, to those who have attained higher things. And Paul writes the like to the Ephesians: "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury." Drunkenness also overturns sobriety and perverts the mind, so that it does not understand what it does. Whence Isaias: Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness; and a little after he adds: "Wine in your feasts, and the work of the Lord you regard not." But they who regard not the works of the Lord, how do they discern between holy and profane, clean and unclean, or how can they exhort and enlighten the people from the Scriptures? Wishing to show the authority of this commandment, he says that God spoke it, that is, inspired it spiritually.

05_marg2109: WHEN YOU ENTER INTO THE TABERNACLE etc. AUGUSTINE. When then was it lawful for them to drink, who needed daily to enter the tabernacle and approach the altar in continual service? For if anyone says that sacrifices were not wont to be laid on every day, what will he say of the daily entry into the tabernacle for the candlestick and for setting the loaves of proposition upon the table? If it is answered that the tabernacle of the testimony is to be understood as that in which was the ark of the testimony, the high priest also needed to enter that for the burning of the incense. For he did not enter once in the year only, but once in the year with the blood of purification, and daily for the incense. Or did God command that they should not drink wine at all? Why then did he not say briefly: You shall not drink wine, but added: When you enter the tabernacle of the testimony etc.? Was it because the cause of not drinking was not to be kept silent, and chiefly because God foreknew that there would afterwards be many, even high priests, at one time, not by succession, who would serve all that ministry in turn, when surely those did not drink whose turn it was to serve, while the others drank? Nothing else is to be understood here, since when he forbade the priests to drink wine and strong drink, he said: A lawful thing for ever in your generations. It is doubtful whether this is connected with the sense before, that is, so that it pertains not to drinking wine, or with the one after, where there follows: To distinguish between the holy and the defiled, the clean and the unclean etc., so that this is the lawful office of the priests for ever in their generations.

05_marg2114: HESYCHIUS. Because every sin is blotted out by penance, and those who committed the aforesaid sin of other doctrine and blasphemy were not saved, the lawgiver sets out the cause of their death. While these things were a doing, the buck goat etc.; because, namely, the sons of Israel and of Aaron did not eat in the holy place what was for sin, that is, did not cause the penance of the sin committed to be performed in the Church. To these this is commanded whom Christ has appointed his vicars in the Church. For he himself offered the blood of his oblation, which was offered for our blood, into the holy place, that is, into heaven, in the sight of the Father. And this sacrifice ought to be eaten in the holy place, that is, the church, for the propitiation of sins. Whence he adds: As was commanded me, that is, as I commanded. For Moses bears the person of Christ. He found it burnt, because they had sinned against the Holy Ghost: the oblation for penance was taken away by the intelligible fire of the Holy Ghost. For to those who sin wilfully there is left no sacrifice for sin. For as true penance merits pardon, so feigned penance provokes God; because the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful. And this the holy Fathers have called the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Ghost: to persevere in crimes to the end of life, to despair of one's salvation, to distrust the power and mercy of the Redeemer.
05_marg2115: While these things were a doing, the buck goat etc. "Not to sin belongs to God alone; to amend, to the wise man"; but rarely will you find one who corrects himself: rare is the confession of sin, rare is penance. Nature and shame resist, because all flesh is liable to fault. And each one blushes to confess his sin, while he thinks more of present things than of future. Moses wishes to find the soul empty of sin, that it may lay down the spoils of error and depart naked of fault without shame of itself; but an unreasoning impulse forestalls it, and the flame of the swiftest motion feeds upon the soul and burns up its innocence. For present things outweigh future, pleasant things serious, glad things sad, and hasty things slower. For iniquity is swift, suggesting occasion to do harm; virtue is slow and delaying, and judges before it begins what is seemly, what is honourable. Iniquity hurries all things headlong. But penance is sluggish and bashful, punished by shame of the present. For it looks only to future things, whose hope is late and whose fruit is slow. Meanwhile shamelessness runs ahead, and penance is shut out by the hope of present things, and its affection is burnt up and abolished. The law seeks it and finds it not. For it is burnt up by the heat and smoke of iniquity. Hence he is angry, and says that penance ought to have been eaten in the holy of holies. He rebukes the priests as sluggish. Aaron answers that the priestly judgment ought to be provident, and that this office is not easily to be entrusted to a conscience not sound, lest the last error be worse than the first. For in a foul vessel either oil or wine is easily spoiled. And how could sin be burnt up in the sight of the Lord, to whom all things are open, where there was strange fire? As if: He does not please God who keeps injustice shut up in his heart and declares that he does penance. Strange fire is lust, avarice and every wicked desire. This fire burns, it does not cleanse. For in whom it is, if they offer in the sight of the Lord, the heavenly fire consumes them, as Nadab and Abiu, together with the things that had been offered for sin. He therefore who wishes to be cleansed, let him remove the strange fire and offer himself to that fire which burns up the fault, not the man. This fire dried up the flowing blood of the woman with the issue of blood; this dried up the fault of the thief. For it is a consuming fire; it heals those who confess simply and purely. Judas said: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood", but he had in his breast the strange fire, inflamed by which he ran to the halter. And he was unworthy of the remedy, because he did not repent with a pure mind. But the priests do not take away the fault of those who offer deceitfully, nor can they feast upon them, whose food is the remission of sins. Whence the true priest says: My meat is to do the will of my Father, that is, that sinners, converted and penitent, be saved. No sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it be true and sincere.
05_marg2116: Truly, since six beasts are commanded to be offered for the people, of which he first mentioned four, the he goat, the ram, the calf and the yearling lamb, of which it is plain that the he goat is for sin, and plain also that the yearling lamb is for a holocaust, let us see whether the two in the middle, the ram and the calf, set down ambiguously, pertained to the sacrifice for sin and were joined to the he goat, or rather to the lamb, so as to be offered in holocaust. What seemed to us on this we have set out. But afterwards, that the six animals might be completed, he mentioned a calf and a ram for the saving sacrifice; and yet in what follows, when they were immolated and mentioned, no mention is made of the ram and calf which he had placed between the goat and the lamb, but only that calf and that ram are mentioned which he had commanded to be offered for the saving sacrifice; so that there would be believed to have been not two beasts but four. Perhaps he named again those two which he had placed before between the he goat and the lamb, and there was not another calf and another ram for the saving sacrifice; so that, when he had said the he goat for sin, and the ram and the calf, not saying for what, and the yearling lamb for a holocaust, he wished afterwards to say what was to be done with the calf and the ram, that is, neither for sin like the he goat nor for a holocaust like the lamb, but they were commanded to be brought in for the saving sacrifice to be burnt. But the question will remain why a he goat was offered for the sin of the Synagogue, when the Lord, speaking from the beginning of the sacrifices which were to be offered for sin, commanded a calf to be offered for the sin of the Synagogue, just as for the sin of the priest, not a goat but a calf; with whose blood, as for the sin of the priest, the horns of the altar of incense were touched; and what the cause was that Moses offered a calf for the sin of Aaron, and Aaron himself another calf, as it behoved to be done for the sin of the priest according to the precept of the Lord. But for the sin of the people not a calf, as had been commanded, but rather a he goat is offered. It seemed to us, therefore, that not the he goat alone was commanded to be offered for the sin of the people, but the ram and the calf also, so that to these three 'for sin' should be understood; because there were also princes among the people, for whom the he goat was to be offered, and individuals could have their own sins, for which the ram; and all one common sin, for which the calf, as it had been commanded from the beginning that a calf should be offered for the sin of the whole Synagogue. And therefore, when they were immolated, he named only the he goat, that the others too might be understood, the whole from a part, all of which had been for sin.

For thereafter they themselves ate the sacrifices for sins. And it is to be believed that Aaron said these things by divine inspiration, which Moses approved as divinely spoken. What then of the other sacrifices of the same day, that is, of the ram and the calf, which we said were also offered for sin? Is there no question of the calf, since it behoved to be done so, that some of its blood should be offered in the holy place, whence the horns of the altar of incense should be touched, and it followed that it should be wholly burnt? What then of the ram? Is it that, because Moses first sought the goat, what was answered about the goat is to be understood also of the ram, which in order he was going to seek, had not the priest's answer pleased him? But what should he seek about the calf, since it could be done under that law which the Lord had commanded about the calf for the sin of the whole Synagogue, as about the calf for the sin of the priest, that is, that it should be wholly burnt without the camp? For Moses in anger said: Why did you not eat what was for sin in the holy place? For since they are holy of holies, it was lawful for you to eat this, that you may take away the sin of the Synagogue and pray for it before the Lord. For none of its blood was brought into the holy place before the face; you shall eat it within, in the holy place etc. When he says: None of its blood was brought into the holy place before the face, he distinguishes that which is done for the sin of the priest or of the Synagogue: not of the goat, of whose blood, since it was not commanded to be brought in to touch the horns of the altar of incense, it ought not to have been wholly burnt but eaten by the priests. 05_marg2129: Morally. Fishes that have fins and scales are wont to leap above the waters. 05_marg2165: SHE SHALL BE UNCLEAN etc. Because, namely, the sower is unclean, as heir of Adam, who was unclean through transgression, and so was mingled with his wife. For after he went out of paradise he knew his wife, and so the human race is propagated. And he defiled life by bringing in the curse and misery and taking away blessedness. 05_marg2166: ON THE EIGHTH DAY etc. The eighth day, since it succeeds the seventh, which is the image of the present life, is a figure of the world to come, in which we shall circumcise the flesh of the foreskin, laying aside all the works of the flesh, no more to sin nor eat nor drink nor marry, because we shall be "as the angels of God". For what "is sown in corruption shall rise in incorruption". It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body. The uncircumcised shall perish from his people, because without circumcision the flesh is abominable and unclean. Circumcision therefore cleanses, in which the resurrection is foreshown. But it is to be noted that the law, commanding circumcision, was silent about its uncleanness. It called the mother unclean until the circumcision, perhaps because Eve was seduced by reason of disobedience; and disobedience brought on us uncleanness and filth.

05_marg2167: THREE AND THIRTY DAYS etc. Seven being added, they make forty. In forty days the male is said to be formed. And two things are proved by these: that the substance of the human race is clean, because it was created by God; therefore he says that the woman sits in clean blood, or the blood of her purification; but because through the succession of Adam's transgression she received seed and conceived, she shall touch no holy thing, nor enter into the sanctuary, until the days of her purging be fulfilled, that is, the forty in which the child is formed. For by the image of God our nature is cleansed, though defiled. We are not commanded, therefore, to enter the sanctuary or touch the holy thing, except because the image of God, once given to our race, afforded entry to the holy things; for the saving of which the Lord was incarnate, and, forty days being fulfilled, he took it up to heaven, as he formed man in the womb, to whom he gave it: then our nature ascended to the true sanctuary. These things are plainly proved by what follows concerning the female sex: for since females are said to be formed in the womb on the eightieth day, he commanded the same number for the fulfilment of the purging or purification of those who receive seed, thus: If she shall bear a maid child, she shall be unclean etc. And it is to be noted that he would not say fourteen days, but two weeks, that in the seven days we may understand human life, and in the monthly flow its affliction, pain and misery. And he well said two weeks, because the female sex is fined double. For she has the whole curse of Adam, and there is added to her: In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children etc. She sits sixty-six days in the blood of her purification, until eighty be fulfilled. For fourteen added to sixty-six make eighty, in which the female is formed. Our race, therefore, defiled by the curse, does not enter into the holy things except through the image of God. For this reason women receiving seed are kept from the holy things during the days of the forming of their little ones; while they have them in the womb they ought not to be kept away. For it is uncertain whether they will bear a female or a male.
05_marg2168: What difference is there between the seven days in which he calls her unclean and the thirty-three in which she shall sit in clean blood? Thus it is read: "To do for him according to the custom of the Law"; it is not said 'for his mother', but "for him", although those things were done which are commanded here concerning two turtles or two young pigeons. 05_marg2172: Our Lord, though he was God, was made for us not only man but also poor, though he was rich, that he might grant us to be partakers of his riches and his divinity. And it is good to consider why these birds above all are commanded to be offered as a victim. For Abraham too, long before the law, offered them for a holocaust, and in very many ceremonies of the law he who is to be cleansed is commanded to be cleansed by them. The dove, then, indicates simplicity, the turtle chastity. For if the turtle by chance lose her mate, she seeks no other after. Whence in the Canticles: "Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's." And elsewhere: "Thy eyes are doves' eyes." Each bird has a moan for its song, and signifies in this the sorrow of the saints, to whom it is said: You shall lament and weep etc. You shall weep, but the world shall rejoice. The simple and modest conversation of the faithful, therefore, is a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord. And he who labours in groaning, who washes his couch with tears, slays a victim most acceptable to God. But because the turtle moans wandering alone, the dove in flocks, the one signifies the secret tears of prayers, the other the assemblies of the Church. The child Jesus is first circumcised, and after an interval of days is brought to Jerusalem with a victim; because, now a young man, he first trod down all corruption of the flesh by dying and rising again; then, after an interval of days, with that same flesh now immortal, which he made a victim for us, he ascended to the heavenly Jerusalem. And each one of us is first cleansed from all sins by the water of baptism, as by a true circumcision, and so, as the grace of the new light advances, enters to the holy altar to be hallowed by the victim of the body and blood of Christ, which, singularly simple and chaste, is figuratively expressed by the immolation of the dove and the turtle. In the prevarication of divine doctrine, using very great distinction, he deals more mildly when speaking of the doctrines of the Jewish law, whose transgression he calls a darkish and shining whiteness. As therefore we call the transgression of the letter of the law a white scar, so let us call ignorance of it a darkish whiteness: not wholly, that is, nor of those things that are common with the law of the Gospel or with the natural law. For these are not venial; but of certain partial and small commandments, such as of the cleansing of a woman in her courses, of the offering of one after childbirth. This ignorance, therefore, as a small scar, he called a darkish whiteness; he who has such ignorance has no need to be cleansed. For these things do not pertain to justice. 05_marg2346: AUGUSTINE. Of the mother, if, conceived by a former husband, she came into the house with the mother; but he forbids dealing with such a sister. If it is not lawful to reveal the shame of a sister from either parent, how much more from both. But what is it that, after the prohibition of lying even with one's granddaughters, whether by son or by daughter, has been set between, there follows: Thou shalt not reveal the nakedness of thy father's wife's daughter. For if he had said thus far, we should understand that lying was forbidden even with the daughter of the stepmother whom the stepmother had borne by a former husband; and she would not be sister, either by father or by mother, to him to whom it is forbidden. But when he added: She is thy sister by the same father, thou shalt not reveal her shame, he makes it manifest that the prohibition was made concerning a sister, since she was of the father and of the stepmother, of whom he had already spoken above; but perhaps he wished to forbid more plainly what he said above obscurely.
05_marg2347: THE DAUGHTER OF THY FATHER'S WIFE etc. AUGUSTINE. Lest he seem to forbid lying with the daughter of a stepmother by a former husband, since she is not sister, either by father or by mother, to him to whom it is forbidden, he added: by the same father.
05_marg2348: THE NAKEDNESS OF THY FATHER'S BROTHER etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether this is forbidden while the brother is living or dead. If while the brother is living, this is contained in the general precept by which a man is forbidden to approach another's wife. Why then does he distinguish the household persons so carefully by their own prohibitions? For what he forbids concerning the father's wife, that is, the stepmother, is not to be taken of the father living, and not rather of the father dead: for while the father lived, who did not know it to be forbidden, since every other man's wife is forbidden? He seems therefore to speak of those persons who, having no husbands, could come together in marriage unless it had been forbidden by the Law, as the custom of the Persians is said to be. But if it is understood to be forbidden when the brother is dead, then no seed will be raised up to the dead brother. It is to be taken thus, therefore: It is not lawful to marry the wife of a deceased brother if the deceased left offspring; or it is forbidden to marry a brother's wife to whom a bill of divorce has been given: for someone might think it lawful for him to marry such a one and not fear adultery.
